solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Acclaim king reversing flow of sea

indicators.note: to reverse something is to run it backwards, so the letters go the other way

blocks.note: CR stands for Carolus Rex, King Charles
the tide is the flow of the sea

explanation.surface: A monarch is praised for turning back the sea, like King Canute.
explanation.walkthrough: The king is not R but CR, Carolus Rex; 'reversing' works only on the tide that follows him.
explanation.definitionFit: To credit someone is to give them praise or recognition for an achievement, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Caught duffer going round university – he’s dealing, I’ll bet

indicators.note: going round something means encircling it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
read as 'more duff': duff and ropy both mean poor or shoddy in British slang
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A useless gambler bluffs about being at college while cheerfully dealing cards and placing bets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duffer' looks like a noun for a bungler, but it is the comparative of the British slang adjective duff, meaning worse, so ROPIER.
explanation.definitionFit: A croupier runs a casino table, dealing cards and taking wagers, which the playful 'I'll bet' confirms.

clue.text: Rearing badger inside box is fine

indicators.note: something inside is held within another thing, so one piece sits in the other
rearing up in a down clue means rising, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the box is British slang for television, and TELE is short for it
to badger someone is to nag them

explanation.surface: An animal stands on its hind legs inside a crate, and someone declares the arrangement fine.
explanation.walkthrough: The badger goes in just after the first letter of the box, and only then is everything read upwards, as a down clue allows.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine can mean refined and graceful in appearance, which is what elegant describes, an adjectival synonym.

clue.text: Start probe into spending limits on Vodafone

indicators.note: the limits of a word are its two ends, so only its outermost letters are taken
spending something means using it up so it is gone, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: to probe into a matter is to investigate it
the first and last letters of the company name

explanation.surface: A regulator launches an inquiry into how much a mobile phone company is spending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spending limits' reads as a single phrase about budgets, but it splits: 'limits on Vodafone' are V and E, and 'spending' removes them from INVESTIGATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To instigate is to set something going or bring it about, so it is a verb synonym for begin.

clue.text: Dragged out Corday’s victim just after ringing hospital

indicators.note: coming just after places one part immediately following another in the line

blocks.note: Charlotte Corday stabbed the French revolutionary Jean-Paul Marat in his bath in 1793
H is the map and road-sign abbreviation for hospital
someone ringing is on the phone, so on stands in for calling

explanation.surface: Charlotte Corday's victim, Marat, is hauled out shortly after somebody phones the hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: Corday murdered the revolutionary Marat in 1793; being on the phone is what 'ringing' means here, and that follows the hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Marathon as an adjective describes something lasting very long and exhausting, like a marathon meeting, so drawn out.

clue.text: George Orwell’s top tip – omit actual suffering

indicators.note: the top of a down entry or word is its first letter, so only that letter is kept
something suffering is in a bad way, damaged and knocked out of shape, so these letters get rearranged

blocks.note: the first letter of the author's name
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice from George Orwell's writing guide: cut out real misery from your prose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'George Orwell' looks like one name, but George is the definition: RAF pilots nicknamed the autopilot George, and Orwell gives only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: George was wartime airmen's slang for the device that flies an aircraft without a pilot's hands, the autopilot.

clue.text: Quickly pop round with one

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: pop and pa are both informal names for a father
an ace is the one in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: Nip round quickly and bring one with you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop round' reads as a casual visit, but it means dad's name turned backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Apace is a slightly old-fashioned adverb meaning at speed or swiftly, so it replaces the definition directly.

clue.text: Cheer try, crowning score? Not half!

indicators.note: a crown sits on top, so in a down entry this part goes above the other

blocks.note: a judge hears or tries a case in court
a score is twenty, and half of twenty is ten

explanation.surface: A rugby fan cheers a try that sits on top of the score, shouting 'Not half!' in delight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much', but here it halves the score of twenty. 'Try' is the legal sense, to hear a case, not rugby.
explanation.definitionFit: To hearten someone is to encourage them and lift their spirits, which is a verb sense of cheer.

clue.text: Thought socially unacceptable outside Italy

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it, so one piece is wrapped around the other

blocks.note: 'not on' is a British idiom for something unacceptable
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: Someone considers a certain kind of behaviour to be frowned upon anywhere outside Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not on' is everyday British for unacceptable, as in 'that's just not on'.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion is an idea or belief held in the mind, so it serves as a noun synonym for thought.

clue.text: Taking lead from Barclays, make smaller bank cards

indicators.note: the lead of a word is what goes in front, its opening letter

blocks.note: to contract is to shrink
the opening letter of the bank's name
a bank of earth is a raised ridge

explanation.surface: Barclays leads the way as banks shrink their branch networks and cut their customers' cards.
explanation.walkthrough: In a clue about Barclays, 'bank' plainly means a lender; it is a ridge of earth that picks up B in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Contract bridge is the standard modern form of the partnership game bridge, played with a full pack of cards.

clue.text: I’m surprised guards head off, showing reason to go to bar

indicators.note: a guard stands around what it protects, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: oh is an exclamation of surprise
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness
a light that is off is out

explanation.surface: Someone gasps as bouncers send a man off, and the cause is his rowdy behaviour in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' is the geographical sense, a promontory. A shout is British and Australian slang for a round of drinks you buy for everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: When it is your turn to buy the round, you have an obvious reason to head up to the pub counter.

clue.text: Adult knocked back gin on his own

indicators.note: to knock something back is to push it backwards, so its letters run in reverse

blocks.note: A is the film classification for adult
a gin is a snare or trap for game

explanation.surface: A grown man sits alone downing his gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back gin' is drinking, but gin here is the old word for a snare, which is then turned around.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone standing apart is separate from others, isolated and alone, an adverbial match for the definition.

clue.text: Bit from ChatGPT’s in AI piece about musician

indicators.note: a bit from something is a small portion of it, so the letters sit inside the run of words
turning about means facing the other way, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the end of the chatbot's name to the start of the last word

explanation.surface: An excerpt from a ChatGPT essay inside an AI article about a musician.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the T of ChatGPT through 'in AI' to the P of 'piece', and are read right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: A pianist plays the piano, so they are a specific kind of musician, an example of the broader class.

clue.text: Harry Potter regularly ignored same wizard

indicators.note: ignoring at regular intervals drops every other letter, keeping only the alternate ones
to harry is to harass and disturb, so these letters are pushed into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters, with the others dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: Harry Potter keeps ignoring the same wizard at Hogwarts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry Potter' is the boy wizard's name, but Harry is the anagram signal and only half of Potter survives.
explanation.definitionFit: A wizard can be a brilliantly skilled expert, and a maestro is a master performer or virtuoso.

clue.text: In passing, former coach bit player

indicators.note: passing means going away, so the little word 'in' departs from what follows

blocks.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
to coach someone is to train them

explanation.surface: A one-time coach is mentioned in passing as having been a minor actor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In passing' reads as 'incidentally', but it tells you IN passes out of TRAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra is a performer with a tiny non-speaking role in a film, which is what a bit player does.

clue.text: American Express accepting PIN missing first element

indicators.note: missing its first means the opening letter is absent and dropped
to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: A is a standard abbreviation for American
to express a view is to state it
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American Express card is accepted, but the PIN is missing, a shop counter mishap.
explanation.walkthrough: American Express looks like the credit card brand; it splits into A and the verb express.
explanation.definitionFit: Astatine is a rare radioactive chemical element, number 85, one of the halogens, so it is an example.

clue.text: Introduction to this no help with EE mobile? It could be

definitions.text: Introduction to this no help with EE mobile? It could be

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so only the opening letter is wanted
mobile means able to move about, so these letters move into a new order

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A customer grumbles that their EE mobile is no help, and wonders what this gadget is.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a mobile from the network EE, a British phone company, could indeed be this.
explanation.definitionFit: A mobile is a portable phone, so a mobile on the EE network is one kind of telephone.

clue.text: Media cover players getting hold of prescribed drug

indicators.note: to get hold of something is to grip it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: the cast are the players in a production
set texts are prescribed ones
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: The press report that some actors were caught with a prescription drug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Media cover' reads as press coverage of the story; it is the definition, a casing that holds recording tape.
explanation.definitionFit: A cassette is a sealed plastic case enclosing magnetic tape, so it literally covers a recording medium.

clue.text: General is charged after Queen’s left protecting Charlie

indicators.note: something that has left is gone, so that letter departs
protecting something means surrounding and shielding it, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: a wire that is charged is electric
R is for Regina, Latin for queen
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A general is put on trial after the Queen departs, while guarding a man called Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' looks like a military rank but is the adjective; 'charged' is electrical, not legal. R comes out of ELECTRIC, then C goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclectic means drawing on a broad, wide-ranging variety of sources, so it matches general in its broad sense.

clue.text: Hard decision over America

blocks.note: an umpire's or referee's call is a decision
O is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for an over
US is short for the United States of America

explanation.surface: A difficult decision about the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like 'concerning', but it is the cricket over, an O on the scorecard.
explanation.definitionFit: A callous person is hard-hearted and unfeeling toward others, matching the emotional sense of the adjective.

clue.text: Pack animal completely around, with minute opening for air

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
the opening of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: all the way means completely
M is the abbreviation for minute
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A beast of burden turns right around and takes a brief moment to come up for air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' could be the adjective meaning tiny, but here it is the unit of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Llamas are South American camelids used in the Andes to carry loads, so they are classic beasts of burden.

clue.text: Swear when held up by mature pedestrian

indicators.note: being held up by something means resting on top of it, so in a down entry this part comes first

blocks.note: to aver is to swear or assert something is true
to mature is to age, as wine or cheese does

explanation.surface: An older man walking along curses when he is mugged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pedestrian' looks like a walker but is the adjective meaning dull; 'held up' is a robbery in the surface but a stacking instruction here.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedestrian as an adjective means ordinary, uninspired and unremarkable, so it is a synonym of middling or mediocre.

clue.text: Pass hour probing what’s on bottom of shoe

indicators.note: a probe pushes inside something, so one piece is inserted into another

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for hour
the tread is the ridged underside of a shoe sole

explanation.surface: Someone spends an hour examining the gunk stuck to the sole of a shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass hour' sounds like killing time, but 'Pass' is the definition, a verb as in threading one's way through a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: To thread through something is to pass carefully through a narrow gap, like a needle or a crowd.

clue.text: English composer reflected about where piece might go

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror appears the wrong way round, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Gustav Holst wrote The Planets
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A composer muses on where a piece of music ought to fit.
explanation.walkthrough: In a clue about a composer, a piece is a musical work; here it is slang for a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A holster is the leather case worn on a belt or under the arm where a gunslinger keeps the handgun.

clue.text: Structure that’s extremely secure except for lock

indicators.note: except means leaving something out, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: a fortified stronghold is a very secure building
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A building that is completely safe apart from its door lock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Except for lock' looks like one phrase, but 'for' is the letters to take away and 'lock' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A lock of hair is a single curl or strand, and a tress is a long lock of a woman's hair.

clue.text: Print newspaper reporter’s opening words?

blocks.note: first meaning: to stamp or imprint a mark onto something
second, playful meaning: the introduction a journalist gives when announcing they are from a newspaper

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: a journalist introducing themselves might say 'I'm press', which runs together into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To impress a design is to stamp it into a surface, so it is a verb synonym for imprint, and the other half splits as I'M PRESS.

clue.text: ‘Ow Dick Turpin made ‘is long journeys gradually diminish?

indicators.note: the dropped H in this cockney spelling tells you to drop every H the same way

blocks.note: the highwayman is referred to as he
the highwayman made his journeys on horseback, Black Bess

explanation.surface: A cockney asks how the highwayman Dick Turpin got about on his long trips.
explanation.walkthrough: Dick Turpin was an 18th-century English highwayman famous for riding his horse. Spoken by a cockney who drops his aitches, 'he rode' becomes ''e rode'.
explanation.definitionFit: To erode is to wear away slowly, as water wears down rock, so it fits a gradual reduction or decline.

clue.text: Awful to-do with Andrew endlessly causing a stink? This could help

definitions.text: causing a stink? This could help

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off
something awful is in a dreadful mess, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the name without its final letter

explanation.surface: A dreadful fuss in which Andrew kicks up a stink, and the clue suggests a remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Causing a stink' reads as making a scene in the surface, but in the definition it means literally smelling bad.
explanation.definitionFit: Deodorant is applied to suppress body odour, so it would help anyone who smells bad.

clue.text: Police officer’s comparatively rapid sacking following debacle

indicators.note: sacking means dismissing, so a letter is thrown out

blocks.note: DI is a detective inspector, plus the 's
faster is the comparative of fast
f is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

explanation.surface: A police officer is swiftly fired after a fiasco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' looks like 'after', but it is the abbreviation f, which the sacking removes.
explanation.definitionFit: A debacle is a sudden humiliating failure or collapse, so a disaster is a close noun synonym.

clue.text: Serious cut close to eye

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter is used

blocks.note: to sever is to cut off
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A grave wound right next to someone's eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as 'near', but it means the close, or end, of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe and serious both describe something grave or harsh in degree, like a severe illness, so they are synonyms.
